ctx.x: See, everything was live music then. There was no radio, and no -- of course, no television. Well, we used to go from Harlem and drive out to Long Island. Honey's wife --

he had a nice house on Bennington Avenue, and his wife, Nellie, she used to cook for us and we'd eat a meal, then we'd drive to where we'd be playing. Mostly it was firemen and policemen's balls. Those people (unintelligible). And, well, it was -- I enjoyed every minute of it.
Honey, he could only play in certain keys, but I knew those keys, and right away, they liked me. So every weekend, there it went, Honey Potter, Honey Potter, Honey Potter.

items.title: 68356_Howard R. Scott oral history interview
items.q: Honey's wife -- he had a nice house on Bennington Avenue, and his wife, Nellie, she used to cook for us and we'd eat a meal

ctx.x: I was still in high school. He said, can you work weekends? I said, oh, yes, sure, sure, sure. He said, well, I'll tell you, you have to come a long way, down on Long Island. He says, but I'll take you out there. He had heard me play, and he said, I could do all right. This fellow was named Honey Potter of Freeport, Long Island. If Honey Potter had been a businessman and had a good education, he could have made a million dollars. He had most of the work out there in Long Island.
See, everything was live music then. There was no radio, and no -- of course, no television. Well, we used to go from Harlem and drive out to Long Island. Honey's wife --

he had a nice house on Bennington Avenue, and his wife, Nellie, she used to cook for us and we'd eat a meal, then we'd drive to where we'd be playing. Mostly it was firemen and policemen's balls. Those people (unintelligible). And, well, it was -- I enjoyed every minute of it.
